e.etymology: A spelling of Eleanor, from Old French Elienor, an adaptation of the Provencal name Alienor. Eleanor of Aquitaine brought it to England in the 12th century; its ultimate meaning is uncertain.

e.meaning: from Gwynedd in Wales; perhaps also fair, blessed
e.etymology: From Gwynedd, the old kingdom and present county of north Wales, perhaps shaped by Welsh gwyn, 'white, fair, blessed'. It became popular in Wales in the 19th century.
namesakes: Gwyneth Paltrow (Oscar-winning actress and founder of Goop)

assoc.t: Gwyneth Paltrow, actress and Goop founder

e.etymology: Yiddish pet form of Malka, Hebrew for 'queen'. It is used mainly in Orthodox and Hasidic Jewish communities.
From the town in Galilee where Jesus grew up. The place name is often linked to Hebrew netser, 'branch, shoot', or natsar, 'to guard', but its origin is not settled.

assoc.t: Nazareth, the town in Galilee where Jesus grew up
Nazareth, the 1970s rock band behind Love Hurts

e.meaning: charm: appeal, or a small token of good luck
e.etymology: From the English word, which came through Old French charme from Latin carmen, 'song, incantation'. Its use as a first name is very recent.

assoc.t: the everyday word, as in lucky charm or charm bracelet

e.etymology: Used in Pakistan and other Muslim communities, where it is usually glossed as 'noble' or 'respected', and in the Philippines. Its linguistic source is not well documented.
A respelling of Giovanni, the Italian form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'. The J spells out the soft Italian G for English and Spanish readers.

In Albanian it is the feminine of Zamir, from ze, 'voice', and mire, 'good'. A separate Central Asian name comes from Arabic damir, 'conscience, heart'. In the US it also reads as a Z- twist on Samira and Amira.
From the Greek Lois of the New Testament, the devout grandmother of Timothy; its meaning is obscure. English Protestants took it up after the Reformation. It is not related to Louise.
namesakes: Lois Lane (reporter and love interest in the Superman stories)
Lois Griffin (the mother on Family Guy)

assoc.t: Lois Lane, reporter in the Superman stories
Lois Griffin, the mother on Family Guy

e.etymology: From Arabic rayhana, a sprig of basil or another fragrant herb. American use took off around 2005 with the Barbadian singer Rihanna, born Robyn Rihanna Fenty.

assoc.t: Rihanna, pop star and Fenty Beauty founder

e.etymology: From Greek Agathe, the feminine of agathos, 'good'. Saint Agatha of Sicily, a third-century martyr, carried the name across Christian Europe.
namesakes: Agatha Harkness (Marvel witch of WandaVision and Agatha All Along)

assoc.t: Agatha Christie, queen of the mystery novel
Agatha Harkness, Marvel witch of Agatha All Along

e.etymology: Taken from the Chevrolet Chevelle, the mid-size car of 1964 to 1977 that is remembered as a muscle car. The model name was a Chevrolet invention with no older meaning.

assoc.t: Chevrolet Chevelle, 1960s and 70s muscle car
Chevelle, hard rock band from Illinois

e.etymology: A Z- spelling of Sadie, the old pet form of Sarah, Hebrew for 'princess'. It was in light use in the 1880s and returned with the novelist Zadie Smith, who changed her own name from Sadie.
e.note: Sounds the same as zayde, the Yiddish word for grandfather.

e.etymology: From a Scottish surname for someone who lived in a glen, Gaelic gleann, 'narrow valley'. As a first name it peaked in mid-20th-century America.
From the Roman name Valentinus, from valens, 'strong, healthy'. Saint Valentine, a third-century martyr, gave his name to the February 14 holiday. In French, Valentine is the feminine form.

assoc.t: Valentine's Day, February 14
a valentine: a love card or a sweetheart

e.etymology: A modern American name, probably a blend of Brent and Brantley; it rose in the early 2010s alongside Brantley and Bentley. It also exists as a rare surname.
A modern American name in the family of Alayah, Malayah and Kaliyah, formed with the popular -ayah ending. No older source is established.
From the Late Latin name Constantia, 'constancy, steadfastness'. The Normans brought it to England, and the Puritans later favored it as a virtue name.

assoc.t: Lake Constance, where Germany meets Switzerland

e.meaning: uncertain; often linked to Italian bella, beautiful
e.etymology: Of uncertain origin: perhaps Italian bella, 'beautiful', with the ending -inda, or an old Germanic name. Alexander Pope made it familiar with the heroine of The Rape of the Lock (1714).
namesakes: Belinda Carlisle (lead singer of the Go-Go's)

assoc.t: Belinda, Mexican pop singer and actress

e.etymology: A spelling of Kaylee, a modern American name built from Kay and the -lee ending, with a push from the popularity of Kayla and Kelly.
A spelling of Carly, a pet form of Carla and Caroline, the feminine forms of Carl, from Germanic karl, 'free man'.
From the name of the Cree, one of the largest Indigenous nations of North America. The word is a French shortening of an Ojibwe name for the people. Cree is also a surname.
namesakes: Cree Summer (actress and voice actress, A Different World)

assoc.t: the Cree, a large Indigenous nation of Canada and the US
Cree LED light bulbs

e.note: It is the name of a living Indigenous nation; some people object to tribal names used as given names.

e.etymology: A recent American coinage that joins the Ky- of Kyrie and Kyree to the -mir ending of Amir and Jamir.
A feminine form of George, from Greek georgos, 'farmer, earth-worker'. It was fashionable in 18th-century England, and Jane Austen gave it to Mr. Darcy's sister in Pride and Prejudice.
namesakes: Georgiana Darcy (Mr. Darcy's sister in Pride and Prejudice)

e.etymology: A spelling of Shea, from the Irish surname O Seaghdha, 'descendant of Seaghdha', a byname thought to mean 'admirable' or 'hawk-like'. Also used as a short form of Shayla and Shaelyn.

assoc.t: Shae, Tyrion's lover in Game of Thrones

e.etymology: From an Irish surname, an Anglicized form of O Caollaidhe, 'descendant of Caollaidhe', a name based on caol, 'slender, graceful'. Keely is the more common American spelling.
namesakes: Keeley Jones (model turned publicist in Ted Lasso)

e.etymology: A modern respelling of Adeline with the -lynn ending. Adeline is a French pet form of Adele, from Germanic adal, 'noble'.

From the word that closes a prayer, Hebrew amen, 'truly, so be it'. Ethiopian and Eritrean Christian families are among those who give it as a name; it can also be a spelling of Arabic Amin, 'trustworthy'.

assoc.t: amen, the word that ends a prayer
Amen or Amun, chief god of ancient Egypt

e.etymology: A Finnish name made popular by a 1907 novel, possibly from Norwegian Eili, a form of Helen, or from Eileen. A separate Hebrew name, Eila or Ela, means 'terebinth tree'. Americans often use it to spell the sound EYE-luh.
French feminine diminutive of Yves, from the Germanic element iv, 'yew', the wood used for bows. English speakers borrowed it in the 19th century.

e.meaning: from Laurentum; linked to the laurel
e.etymology: A short form of Lorenzo or Laurence and, for girls, a spelling of Lauren. All go back to the Latin Laurentius, 'man from Laurentum', a town whose name is tied to laurus, 'laurel'.

assoc.t: Sophia Loren, Italian film star (surname)

e.etymology: The Spanish form of Estelle and Stella, from Latin stella, 'star', by way of Occitan estela. Saint Estelle was a third-century martyr.
